en: Oṃ. Now begins the fifth chapter;
now begins the first Brāhmaṇa of the fifth chapter. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.1.1)
That is full, this is full; from the full, the full is drawn forth.
When the full of the full is taken away, the full alone remains.
Space is Brahman.
"Space is ancient;
space is the wind," so indeed said Kauravyāyaṇīputra.
The Brahmins know this as the Veda;
by means of this Veda, that which is to be known is known.
"Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya 5.1.1: 'Full is that, full is this'—this means it is pervasive and not excluded from anything.
Furthermore, the suffix [of the word *pūrṇam*] should be understood as having an agentive sense (*kartari*).
The pronoun *adaḥ* (that) is an indefinite term denoting something remote."
That is the meaning of "the Supreme Brahman.

That is complete, all-pervading like space, continuous, and without limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika). That very same [Brahman], when possessed of adjuncts, abiding in name and form, and having entered into empirical usage, is full by its own nature as the Supreme Self, pervading [all] precisely as such; it is not [full] by means of a specific self limited by adjuncts.
This very Brahman, having attained a specific state as an effect (*kāryātmaka*), emerges, rises up, and issues forth from the full causal self (*kāraṇātman*).

Although it emerges in the form of an effect, nevertheless it does not abandon its own nature—its fullness and its state as the Supreme Self (*paramātmabhāva*); rather, it emerges while remaining full.
Having taken—that is, grasped—the fullness of the full Brahman in the form of the effect, and having attained the state of being of a single essence with its own true nature, [it emerges].

By means of knowledge (*vidyā*), having set aside the appearance of otherness—which is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*) and born from association with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the mere elements (*bhūtamātra*)—there remains only the absolute Brahman, which is full, without interior or exterior, and whose essential nature is a single mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*) and uniform flavor.
This is the meaning of the mantra: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself, therefore it became all.
In this context, the meaning of the word "Brahman" is expressed by the phrase "This is full" (*pūrṇam ada*).
"This is full" means that Brahman indeed was this in the beginning;
thus says another Śruti: "What is here, that is there; what is there, that is here.

Therefore, that which is denoted by the word "that" (adaḥ) is the full Brahman; that very same [Brahman] is this full [world] existing as an effect, conjoined with the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of name and form, and augmented by ignorance (avidyā).
Therefore, that which appears as if other than the very nature of the ultimate reality—

when one has known that very Self as the supreme, full Brahman, thinking "I am this full Brahman," and having thus taken up the fullness while casting aside the state of being incomplete produced by ignorance, born from contact with the limiting adjuncts of name and form— by means of this knowledge of Brahman...
Only the Full remains.
Thus it has been said: "Therefore, that became all.
That which is the meaning of all the Upanishads—namely Brahman—is restated by this mantra for the purpose of connecting with what follows.

For the means—namely *oṃkāra*, self-restraint (*dama*), charity (*dāna*), and compassion (*dayā*)—which are about to be described as the instruments for the knowledge of Brahman, are intended to be taught; and because they belong to the supplementary section (*khila-prakaraṇa*), they are auxiliary to all forms of meditation (*upāsanā*).
Regarding this, some explain as follows: from the full cause, the full effect is impressed;
even in the present time, that impressed effect remains full, being the ultimate reality in the form of duality.
Furthermore, at the time of dissolution, having taken up the fullness of the effect and withdrawn it into itself, only the cause in its causal form remains as fullness.
Thus, in all three times—origination, persistence, and dissolution—the fullness alone belongs to both the effect and the cause.
And that single fullness is designated by different names according to the distinction between effect and cause.
Thus, Brahman is one, consisting of both duality and non-duality.
Just as the ocean indeed consists of water, waves, foam, bubbles, and so forth;

and just as the water is real, while the waves, foam, bubbles, and the like arising from it—which possess the nature of appearance and disappearance—are essentially of the nature of the ocean and are themselves ultimately real.

Thus, all this duality is indeed the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*) in the same way that waves and so forth are [real] as the ocean water; the Supreme Brahman alone is like the ocean water itself.

And so, it is said, while the Karmakāṇḍa possesses authority when duality is real, when duality—like a mirage—is unreal, being produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), and non-duality alone is the ultimate reality, then the Karmakāṇḍa becomes non-authoritative due to the absence of its object.
And thus, there would indeed be a contradiction:

the Upaniṣads, being a portion of the Veda, would be authoritative because they establish the reality of ultimate non-duality, whereas the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) would be non-authoritative because its subject matter is unreal duality.

Desiring to avoid this contradiction, the Śruti has stated through such passages as "Full is this, full is that" (*pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam*) that both cause and effect possess reality, like the ocean.
That is incorrect, because it is impossible for there to be either a denial or a conceptual construction regarding a qualified object;
for this is not a well-conceived hypothesis.
Why? Because, just as an exception (*apavāda*) is made for a specific portion of a general rule (*utsarga*) regarding the scope of an action— for example,

"not harming any living beings except at sacred sites" (*tīrtha*), where the harming of all beings, though prohibited by the general rule, is permitted in the specific domain of the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and the like.

Furthermore, non-duality (*advaita*) regarding the reality of things cannot be established here by first teaching Brahman as a general principle and then subsequently negating it in respect to one part of it;
for precisely because Brahman is non-dual, the existence of "parts" is untenable,
and likewise, conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) is impossible.

Just as in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, where one either takes it at the *atirātra* sacrifice or does not take it at the *atirātra* sacrifice, an option (*vikalpa*) arises because the taking or not taking depends upon the person;
however, here in the case of the objective reality, an option such as "is there duality or non-duality" is not possible, because the reality of the Self is independent of the person.
Furthermore, there is a contradiction between the two states of duality and non-duality within a single entity.
Therefore, this conceptualization is not well-conceived,
as it contradicts both scripture and logic;
for [the Self] is a solid mass of consciousness, of a single uniform essence like a block of salt, continuous and devoid of distinctions such as before and after, or outer and inner.
All such scriptural passages as "without interior or exterior," "unborn," "not this, not this," "neither gross nor subtle," "unborn, undecaying, fearless, immortal"—

whose meanings are certain and free from the suspicion of doubt or error— would become as if cast into the ocean, being rendered ineffective. Likewise, there is also a contradiction with logic (*nyāya*), because it is impossible for that which possesses parts, is manifold in nature, and is active to be eternal.
Furthermore, the permanence of the self is inferred from the observation of memory and so forth;
if it were impermanent, there would be a contradiction with that [observation],
and your hypothesis would be rendered purposeless.

Moreover, on this view, the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) of the Veda would clearly be rendered useless, due to the consequence that one would experience the results of actions not performed and that actions performed would perish without result.

Now, an objection may be raised: "Since there are scriptural illustrations such as the ocean [which possesses both unity and diversity], Brahman can consist of both duality and non-duality; why then do you say that it is contradictory for a single entity to possess both duality and non-duality? We reply: No.
Because it pertains to a different subject matter.
For we have stated that contradiction concerns eternal, partless entities, such as duality and non-duality, and not regarding effects which possess parts.
Therefore, this conception is untenable due to its conflict with scripture, tradition, and logic.
It would be better to abandon this [Upaniṣadic] conception altogether than to accept it; furthermore, this conception does not constitute the meaning of the scripture,

because the Upaniṣads do not teach that Brahman— being agitated by hundreds of thousands of varieties of misfortunes such as birth and death, possessing parts like the ocean or a forest, and having many flavors— is an object of meditation or an object of knowledge.
And it teaches the state of being a single mass of consciousness,
saying, "It should be seen as one alone," and because it negates the perception of multiplicity by stating, "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity."
And that which is censured by the Śruti must not be performed;
and that which is not performed is not the meaning of the scripture.
Therefore, the multiplicity of flavors and the multiplicity of constituent parts of Brahman, which take the form of duality, should not be perceived, because they have been censured.
Therefore, that is not the meaning of the scripture (*śāstra*).
However, the fact that Brahman is of a single essence (*ekarasa*) is praiseworthy because it is what is to be seen; and because it is praiseworthy, it is fit to be the meaning of the scripture.

As for what was said—that a portion of the Veda lacks authority regarding the subject of ritual action (*karma*) due to the absence of duality, while it possesses authority regarding non-duality (*advaita*)—[that is incorrect].
That is not so,
because the purpose [of the scripture] is to teach according to what has been attained [by the student].
For the scripture does not first inform a person— whether of duality or non-duality— as soon as he is born, and only afterwards instruct him in ritual action or the knowledge of Brahman.
Furthermore, duality is not fit to be taught because it is accessible to the intellect of any living being as soon as it is born.
Nor could anyone possess, from the very outset, the realization that duality is unreal;
for if that were so, the scripture would first teach the reality of duality and only afterwards establish its own authority regarding the Self.
Nor would even those established by heretics fail to accept the authority of the scripture.

Therefore, taking as its basis the duality produced by ignorance—which is innate and natural—the scripture teaches action as a means to achieve the desired human goals for one who is joined with that innate ignorance and possessed of defects such as passion and hatred; it does so first, and subsequently for one who perceives the defects in the nature of actions, their factors, and their fruits, as they are commonly understood.

For one who desires the fruit of abiding in the nature of indifference, which is the opposite of that [bondage], he teaches the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), consisting in the realization of the oneness of the Self, as the means to that end. Now, this being so, once the fruit— abiding in the nature of that indifference— is attained, the scripture's status as an authoritative means ceases its demand for further action.
Due to the absence of that [duality], even the status of being a scripture ceases to exist for him; thus,
since the scripture is complete with respect to each individual person, there is not even a scent of contradiction with the scripture,
because the distinctions of duality— such as the scripture, the disciple, and the teaching— culminate in the knowledge of non-duality (*advaita*).

For there would be a contradiction if any one of them were to remain [while the others were absent], because the teacher, the disciple, and the teaching are mutually dependent; yet, since none of them remains [in isolation], when everything has reached its completion, of what could a contradiction be suspected? This is so when non-duality alone, which is auspicious, is established.
Nor, for that very reason, is there even a state of non-contradiction.
Moreover, even granting [your position], we say that the contradiction with scripture remains equal;
for even when Brahman alone is non-dual in nature—like the ocean—and nothing else exists, it is still contradicted.
Insofar as there is mutual instruction regarding the sphere of duality, such that "this is one thing" and "duality is another," the analogy of the ocean is contradictory.

Furthermore, just as in the case of the oneness of the ocean's water, if consciousness were a single unity, it would be impossible to conceive of the teaching and receiving of instruction occurring in different locations from Brahman.

For instance, in the case of Devadatta—who consists of both duality and non-duality through his hands and other limbs—his speech, being a part of Devadatta, is the teacher, while his ear alone is the receiver of the instruction; Devadatta himself, however, is neither the teacher nor the receiver of the instruction.
It is possible to conceive [this],
because Devadatta possesses a single consciousness, just as the ocean has the nature of being a single body of water.
Therefore, such a conception would result in both a contradiction of scripture and logic, and the failure to establish the intended meaning.
Therefore, the meaning of the mantra "pūrṇam adaḥ" is exactly as we have explained.
Furthermore, this mantra "oṃ khaṃ brahma," which is not prescribed for other purposes elsewhere, is here employed by the Brāhmaṇa for the practice of meditation.
In this context, "brahman" is the substantive designation and "kha" (the void/space) is the qualifier.
Furthermore, there is a designation of the qualifier and the qualified through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in "the sky is Brahman" (*khaṃ brahma*) like "the blue lotus.
The word *brahman*, which refers generally to any vast entity without specific qualification, is therefore specified as "Brahman is the sky.

That which is the sky-Brahman is denotable by the word *oṃ*; whether it is understood as being expressible by the word *oṃ* or as having the very nature of the sound *oṃ*, in both ways the coreferentiality is not contradictory.

And here, the word *oṃ* is employed for the purpose of serving as a means for the meditation on Brahman. This is evident from other scriptural passages such as: "This support is the best; this support is the supreme"; "One should yoke the Self with *oṃ*"; "With this very syllable *oṃ*, one should meditate upon the Supreme Person"; and "Thus, meditate upon the Self as *oṃ*," and so forth.
Furthermore, because no other purpose for the instruction is possible—

just as in other instances such as "He praises with 'Om'," "He sings the Udgītha with 'Om'," and so forth, where the employment of the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and conclusion of Vedic study is understood from its specific application (*viniyoga*)— and since no such other purpose is understood here,
the instruction regarding the word *oṃ* in this context is solely for the purpose of being a means to meditation.

Although words such as *brahman*, *ātman*, and so forth are denotators of Brahman, nevertheless, according to the authority of the Śruti, the syllable *oṃ* (Oṃkāra) is the closest designation of Brahman.
For this very reason, it is the supreme means for the realization of Brahman.
And that [realization] occurs in two ways: by way of being a symbol (*pratīka*) and by way of being a name (*abhidhāna*).
Just as [Brahman is perceived] through various images such as those of Viṣṇu and others by way of a symbol (*pratīka*),
so too should the syllable *oṃ* be understood as Brahman;
for indeed, Brahman becomes gracious to one who takes *oṃ* as his meditative support (*ālambana*).
"‘This is the best object of focus, this is the supreme object of focus;
having known this object of focus, one is glorified in the world of Brahman’—so says the Śruti.

In that context, [the word] ‘space’ (kha) is used so that there may be no understanding of it as physical space; thus he says ‘ancient space’ (purāṇaṃ khaṃ), meaning the space that is the Supreme Self (paramātmākāśa).”

That which is the ancient space (kha) of the Supreme Self is without support and impossible to grasp because it is not an object of the eyes and other senses; therefore, through faith, devotion, and a particular state of being, one causes the syllable Om to enter it, just as people in the world [visualize] Viṣṇu in a stone or other image marked with the signs of Viṣṇu.
"Vāyuraṃ khaṃ" means that space (kha) in which wind (vāyu) exists is "vāyuraṃ khaṃ"; he said that "kha" refers merely to space (khamātra), not to the ancient space (purāṇaṃ kha). Thus he spoke.
Who is he?
He is Kauravyāyaṇīputra.
For wind is primary in the sky; since it is designated by its own specific term [vāyu], he considers it appropriate that the understanding [of the word "speech"] refers to the mouth.

In this regard, whether the "ancient ether" (*purāṇaṃ kham*) is Brahman in its nature devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhisvarūpa*), or the "ether consisting of air" (*vāyuraṃ kham*) is Brahman with limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*), in either case the syllable *Oṃ* serves as a means by way of being a symbol (*pratīka*), like an image [of a deity].
This is because of another scriptural passage: "O Satyakāma, this *Oṃ* is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman."
There is only a disagreement regarding the specific meaning of its own word:
"Veda" is this syllable *oṃ*; one knows by means of it that which is to be known.
Therefore, the syllable *oṃ* is the Veda, the designator, the signifier.
By means of that designation, the practitioner understands and perceives Brahman—that which is to be known, which is being revealed, and which is being designated.
Therefore, the Brahmins know: "This is the Veda.
Consequently, it is intended that the syllable *oṃ* serves as the means of realization by virtue of being the designation for the Brahmins.
Alternatively, the passage beginning with "This is the Veda" is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
How is it that the syllable *oṃ* is prescribed as a symbol (*pratīka*) of Brahman?
Through the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the statement "Oṃ Khaṃ Brahman," its praise is now expressed by way of its being the Veda.
For this entire Veda is indeed the syllable *oṃ*.

Originating from this and having this as its essence, the whole Veda—divided into the distinctions of *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, *Sāman*, and so forth—is the syllable *oṃ* alone; for another scriptural passage states: "Just as all leaves are held together by a stalk," and so on.
Furthermore, this Veda is the syllable *oṃ* because whatever is to be known, all that which is to be known is the Veda, which is the syllable *oṃ*.
For this very reason, the other Veda also possesses the status of being a Veda;
therefore, this *oṃkāra* should be understood as a distinguished means of accomplishment.
Alternatively, it is itself the Veda.
Who is he?
He whom the Brahmins know as the *vidura* from the syllable *oṃ*;
for he is to be known by the Brahmins through various conceptualizations such as the *praṇava*, the *udgītha*, and so forth.
For when that [Veda] is employed as the means of accomplishment, the entire Veda becomes employed. //1//
Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Śrī Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad Bhāṣya.
There were three descendants of Prajāpati who lived the life of a religious student under their father Prajāpati:
the gods, humans, and the asuras.
Having lived the holy life, the gods said, "May your honor speak to us.
To them he spoke this syllable: "Da. [The gods asked: "Have you understood? "Yes," he replied.
"We have understood," they said. "You have told us, 'Be self-controlled'. "Yes," he said, "you have understood. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.2.1)
Now this section begins for the purpose of prescribing the triad of means beginning with self-restraint (*dama*). "Three" means numbering three;

"prājāpatyas" means offspring of Prajāpati. What [did they do]? Being disciples—since the state of being a disciple is primary in the practice of *brahmacarya* toward their father Prajāpati—they lived the life of *brahmacarya*; that is the meaning of "they dwelt."
Who were they? Specifically, the gods, humans, and asuras.
Having lived the life of religious studentship (*brahmacarya*), what did they do? This is stated: those gods spoke to their father, Prajāpati.
"What is it? [they asked].
"Tell us, speak to us what your instruction is.
To those who were thus seeking, he spoke this single syllable, merely a phoneme: "Da."

Having spoken thus, the father asked them: "Did you understand?"—that is, "Have you understood the meaning of the syllable uttered by me for the purpose of instruction, or not? The gods replied, "We have understood; we have understood it."
"If that is so, tell me what I said.
The gods replied, "By nature you are self-controlled; therefore, you told us, 'Become self-controlled,' thus speaking to us.
The other said, "Yes; you have understood correctly. //1//
Then the men said to him, "May your honor speak to us.
To them he spoke this very syllable: "Da."
"Did you understand?
"We understood," they said. "Then did you say to us, 'Give'?"
"Om," he said, "you have understood. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.2.2)
The rest is the same.
"Since you are by nature greedy, therefore, as far as your ability permits, share with us and give," thus did he say to us; what else could he have said for our benefit? Thus say the men. 2.
Then the Asuras said to him, "May your honor speak to us.
To them he spoke this very syllable: "Da."
"Did you understand?
"We understood," they said. "Then why do you say to us, 'Be compassionate'?"
"Om," he said, "you have understood.
This very same divine voice, the thunder, repeats this: *da-da-da*, which means:
"Be self-controlled, give, be compassionate."
Therefore, one should train in these three: self-restraint, generosity, and compassion.
Likewise, he said to the Asuras, "Be compassionate.
[The meaning is: "Since you are cruel and intent upon violence and the like, therefore be compassionate; show mercy toward living beings.
This very instruction of Prajāpati continues to prevail even today.

He who was formerly Prajāpati and instructed the gods and others still instructs even today by means of divine speech characterized by thunder. How is this divine speech heard? What is that thunder? It is uttered three times as the syllable "da"—"da-da-da"—as an indicator for these sentences: "Be self-controlled (dāmyata)," "Give (datta)," and "Be compassionate (dayadhvam). This is an imitation, and not the actual sound of thunder;
for a restriction to exactly three repetitions is not established in common worldly usage.

Because even today Prajāpati still instructs, "Restrain yourselves, give, and be compassionate," for that reason these three—what are those three? It is said: self-restraint (*dama*), charity (*dāna*), and compassion (*dayā*). One should train in them, one should adopt them; one should form the thought, "The instruction of Prajāpati must be carried out by us.
And so says the *Smṛti*: "This threefold gate of hell leads to the destruction of the self."
"Lust, anger, and likewise greed—one should therefore abandon these three.
For this [latter] injunction is indeed a supplement to the former.
Nevertheless, for what purpose did Prajāpati utter the triad of *da* syllables with reference to the gods and others, when they were already seeking separate instructions?

Or rather, how did they practice through discernment? Those who know the intentions of others speculate: "By means of the mere sound of the letter *da*, which was identical [to the one previously taught], they grasped what was in Prajāpati’s mind.

Regarding this, some say: because they were untamed, arrogant, and lacking in compassion, they considered themselves at fault; thus, filled with apprehension, they remained near Prajāpati, wondering, "What will he say to us?
And for them, by the mere hearing of the letter *da*, an understanding of its meaning arose through the force of their own inner anxiety.

For it is well known even in the world that sons and disciples, being those who are to be instructed, must be turned away from faults. Therefore, it is appropriate that Prajāpati uttered only the syllable *da*. And because the three qualities beginning with self-restraint (*dama*) contain the letter *da*, one may understand the gods and others through their distinction according to the nature of one's own faults.
The fruit of this, however, is that once one has knowledge of the defects of the self, those defects can be eliminated even with a brief instruction—such as by the mere syllable *da*.

Now, it might be argued: "This instruction for the three classes beginning with the gods is such that each one of them, even today, should adopt only one [of the three], and not all three; therefore, humans should not train in all three.
To this it is replied: Even by the ancient beings beginning with the gods, only one was to be adopted, and even today, humans should not train in all three.
Alternatively, there exist no gods, asuras, or others whatsoever apart from human beings.

Among humans themselves, those who are undisciplined yet endowed with other superior qualities are "gods"; those dominated by greed are "humans"; and likewise, those intent on violence and cruel are "asuras. It is these very same humans who, in view of the three defects such as lack of self-restraint, receive the specific designations of "god" and so forth.
And other qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—also exist in relation to one another.
Therefore, this triad must be practiced by humans alone, because it was taught by Prajāpati specifically with reference to them.
For indeed, humans are seen to be undisciplined, greedy, and cruel.
And likewise, the Smṛti says: "Lust, anger, and greed—therefore, one should abandon these three. (3)
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya.
This heart is Prajāpati;
this is Brahman.
All this is that very three-syllabled heart: *hṛ* is one syllable; *daya* is two syllables. Thus, "heart" (*hṛdayam*) consists of these three syllables.
*Hṛ* is one syllable.
Both his own people and others bring gifts to him who knows this.
"Da" is one syllable;
both his own people and others give to him who knows this.
"Yam" is one syllable;
he who knows this goes to the heavenly world. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.3.1)

The triad of means beginning with self-control (dama) has been prescribed as supplementary to all meditations (*upāsana*). One who is self-controlled, free from greed, and compassionate is qualified for all meditations.

Therein, the vision of Brahman without attributes (*nirupādhika*) has already been discussed; now, however, follow the meditations upon that same Brahman with attributes (*sopādhika*), which have prosperity (*abhyudaya*) as their fruit.
This undertaking is for the purpose of stating what must be said: it was just stated that "this Prajāpati is that which is visible; Prajāpati instructs.
But who is this instructor, Prajāpati?
It is replied: he is this Prajāpati.
Who is this "heart"? By "heart" is meant the intellect (*buddhi*) situated in the heart.

That very heart—which was described at the end of the *Śākalyabrāhmaṇa* as the locus of names, forms, and actions through the division of the quarters, and which is established in all beings and has become the self of all beings—is Prajāpati, the creator of creatures.
This is Brahman, because of its vastness (*bṛhattva*) and because it is the self of all;
this is everything.
That the heart is everything has been stated in the fifth chapter.
Since all that [is contained] therein, therefore the Heart is to be meditated upon as Brahman.
First, the meditation concerning the syllables of the name "Heart" (hṛdaya) itself is stated:
this name "Heart" consists of three syllables; it has three syllables (*tryakṣaram*).
What, then, are those three syllables?
"Hṛ" is one syllable.
He who knows that this form "hṛ" belongs to the root *hṛ*, which has the sense of bringing (*āhṛti*), [knows] for the sake of the Brahman that is the heart.
One's own sense organs and other objects such as sound bring their respective effects; and the heart brings [all things] for the sake of the enjoyer.
Therefore, for one who knows that this syllable "hṛ" is the name of the heart, both his own kinsmen and others unrelated to him bring offerings to that wise man.
The word "offering" (*bali*) is the completion of the sentence.
This fruit corresponds to consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Likewise, this single syllable "da" is also derived from the root *dadāti* (to give), meaning "giving. This form "da" is established as a syllable of the name "Heart" (*hṛdaya*). Here too, for the sake of the Heart—the Brahman—both one's own instruments (the senses) and other objects give their respective vigor (*vīrya*), and the Heart gives its own vigor to the enjoyer; therefore, it is the letter "da. Thus...
Both his own people and others give to him.
Likewise, "yam" is also a single syllable;
he who knows that this form of the root *i*, meaning "to go," is bound within this name, goes to the heavenly world.

If such a distinguished fruit is obtained even from a single syllable of the Name, what need is there to mention the fruit obtained from the meditation on the essential nature of the Heart? Thus, the mention of the syllables of the Name is for the purpose of praising the Heart. //1//
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the commentary on the venerable Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
That indeed was this very thing;
it was simply the Real (satya).

He who knows this great, first-born being as the True Brahman conquers these worlds; indeed, that [other world] becomes conquered for him who thus knows this great, first-born being as the True Brahman.
For Brahman is indeed the Truth.

Desiring to enjoin the meditation on that very Brahman called the heart as "Truth," [the text] says: "That—that is the heart. The word "that" refers back to the heart as Brahman. The particle "vā" is for the purpose of recollection; thus, one "that" (tat) indicates that the heart is being recalled as Brahman. The second "that" (tat) refers to the fact that it is being meditated upon. Thus, there is one "that" (tat).
This is what is expressed by the phrase "in another way" (*prakārāntareṇa*); this is the second occurrence of the word *tat*. What, then, is that other way?
It is connected with the third occurrence of the word *tat* in the expression "this very thing is that" (*etadeva tat*).

Bringing to mind what is about to be stated with the word "this," he says: "it was" (āsa), meaning it existed. But what was it that existed? It is that which was called "the heart is Brahman"; thus, the third occurrence of the word "that" (tat) is employed.

He specifies what that is in detail: "Truth indeed is both *sat* (the existent) and *tyat* (the beyond), both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*); Truth is Brahman, consisting of the five elements.

Whoever knows this very Self of Truth—the Great One (*mahat*) because of its magnitude, the Worthy of Worship (*yakṣa*), the First-born (*prathamaja*), born before all that pertains to transmigratory existence, since this Brahman was born first, therefore it is the First-born—who knows it, who understands it as "Brahman is Truth."

The fruit of this is stated as follows: Just as by means of Truth these worlds were made one's own and conquered by Brahman, so he who knows the Great Yakṣa, the first-born Brahman whose self is Truth, conquers these worlds. Furthermore, "he is conquered," meaning he is brought under control;
"this enemy"—this is the completion of the sentence—meaning that enemy becomes non-existent, i.e., he is conquered.
He concludes again by asking, "To whom does this fruit belong?"—namely, to one who knows this great being, the first-born, as the True Brahman.
Therefore, it is logical that the fruit corresponds to the knowledge;
for Brahman is indeed the Truth. //1//
Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the commentary on the venerable Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
In the beginning, this world was indeed water alone. Those waters created the Real (satya).
Truth is Brahman;
Brahman [created] Prajāpati;
Prajāpati [created] the gods.
Those gods worship truth alone.
This [word] consists of three syllables: *sa-ti-ya-m*. *Sa* is one syllable;
*ti* is one syllable.
The syllable "yam" consists of three letters.
The first and last letters are truth, while the middle one is untruth.
Thus, this untruth is enclosed on both sides by truth.
It becomes nothing but truth;
falsehood does not harm one who knows this. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.1)
This is said for the purpose of praising Brahman as Truth.
It was stated that [Brahman] is "the great, first-born Yakṣa"; how, then, is it the first-born?
It is explained: "In the beginning, this world was indeed water."
"Water" refers to the oblations of the Agnihotra and other rites which are inherent in the action.
Because the oblations of the Agnihotra and other rites consist of liquid matter, they possess the nature of water.

And these waters, after the completion of the Agnihotra and other rites, do not exist in isolation; rather, while not abandoning their state of being inherent in the action through some unseen subtle essence, they exist only in conjunction with the other elements.

However, because they are the substratum of karma, water is primary. All elements, prior to their manifestation, are designated as "water" when they exist in an undifferentiated state together with the agent. Those waters, existing as the seed of the world in an undifferentiated form, were indeed this entire world differentiated by name and form at the beginning; there was nothing else whatsoever born of modification.
Those waters, in turn, created truth;
therefore, truth is the first-born Brahman.
This is the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha, the Sūtrātman, which is the manifestation of the undifferentiated world.
Why is that Truth Brahman?
Because of its greatness. How is there greatness? He says:
Because he is the creator of all.
How so?
That which is the true Brahman created Prajāpati, the lord of creatures, namely Virāj, who possesses the sun and other instruments; this is to be supplied as the grammatical connection.
Prajāpati, that Virāj Prajāpati, created the gods.
Since everything has thus been born in sequence from the true Brahman, therefore the great Brahman is the Truth. But how is it a Yakṣa?
It is said: those gods, having been thus created, even transcending their father Virāj, meditate upon that very same Truth, Brahman.
Therefore, this is the first-born, the great Yakṣa.
For that reason, it is to be worshipped with one's whole being; and the name of that Truth-Brahman is "Satyam" (Truth). This consists of three syllables.
He asks, "What are those syllables? and says: *sa* is one syllable; *ti* is one syllable; the following vowel *ī* is for the purpose of indicating [the preceding consonant].
The word "yam" consists of a single syllable.
Among its constituent letters, the first and the last— the letter *sa* and the letter *ya*— are truth,
because they lack the nature of death.
In the middle is falsehood;
for death is indeed falsehood,
because of the commonality of the letter *t* between "death" (*mṛtyu*) and "falsehood" (*anṛta*).

This very syllable *takāra*, which is false and of the nature of death, is enclosed on both sides by the two syllables *sakāra* and *yakāra*—which are characterized as truth—and is thus pervaded and contained within them.
Therefore, being of the nature of truth, it becomes powerless; indeed, it results in an abundance of truth (*satyabhūya*), that is, a preponderance of truth.
Thus, for one who knows this—the preponderance of truth and the powerlessness of all falsehood and death—that falsehood, even if spoken through inadvertence, does not harm him. //1//
Now, that which is the Real is yonder sun;
the person who is in this orb and the person who is here in the right eye— these two are established in one another.
By means of its rays, this [sun] is established in this [body], and by means of the vital breaths, this [body] is established in that [sun].
When he is about to depart, he sees this orb as pure;
these rays do not return to him.
Now, the meditation upon the specific configuration of this Satya Brahman is being described: "That which...
What is that Satya Brahman, the first-born?
Is it this [sun]? Who is this Āditya? Furthermore, who is this Āditya who is the person (puruṣa) presiding within this solar disc? He is that very Satya Brahman.
And this person who is within the self, who is this person in the right eye—he too, by virtue of the word "and" (ca), is connected to the statement that he is the true Brahman.

Since these two persons—the one situated in the sun and the one situated in the eye—are specific manifestations of the one true Brahman, therefore they are in each other: the solar person in the ocular person, and the ocular person in the solar person.
They are established;
for the internal (adhyātma) and the divine (adhidaivata) are mutually supportive.
How are they said to be established? This sun, bestowing favor through its rays and its light, is established in this internal [eye], which pertains to the eye.
And this visual [self], supporting the sun by means of the vital breaths, is established in that sun as the divine substrate (adhidaiva).

When he— the enjoyer consisting of consciousness within this body— is about to depart at a certain time, then that solar person in the eye withdraws his rays and remains in a state of pure neutrality.
Then this one consisting of consciousness sees only the pure, absolute, and rayless orb, like the orb of the moon.
This vision of the omen (ariṣṭa) is shown incidentally so that a person might indeed be diligent regarding what ought to be done.

It is not with reference to this person seen in the eye that these rays, which previously came toward him for the sake of favoring him by the power of their master's duty, now fail to reach or return to him as if constrained by the exhaustion of his karma;
therefore, it is understood from their mutual relationship of helper and helped that these two are indeed portions of the one true Self alone. //2//
Of this person who is in that orb, "bhūḥ" is the head;
there is one head, and this syllable is one.
"Bhuvaḥ" refers to the two arms;
these two arms are these two syllables.
"Svaḥ" refers to the foundation.
These two syllables have two foundations. Their secret name (upaniṣad) is "Ahar.
He who knows this destroys evil and leaves it behind. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.3)
In that context, regarding that person who is within this orb—whose name is Satya—his constituent parts are the *vyāhṛtis*.
How so?
This *vyāhṛti* which is "Bhūḥ" is his head.
Because of its primacy, the Scripture itself declares the commonality therein: "The single head is the syllable *bhūḥ*, being joined with the number one;
the two arms are *bhuvaḥ*, because of the commonality of duality—there are two arms and these are two syllables."
Likewise, "Sva" is the foundation; these two syllables are two foundations, for one stands firm by means of them—these being the feet.
This is the secret name (*upaniṣad*), the hidden designation, of this very Brahman which consists of the parts of the *vyāhṛtis* and is Truth.
By means of that designation by which Brahman is designated, one becomes oriented toward that Brahman, as is the case in common worldly usage.
What is it? He says: "Day! Day! This form [of the word] comes from the roots *han* (to strike) and *hā* (to abandon). He who knows this strikes away and abandons evil—provided he knows thus. //3//
This person who is in the right eye— his head is "bhūḥ.
There is one head, and this syllable is one.
"Bhuvaḥ" refers to the two arms;
these two arms are these two syllables.
"Svaḥ" refers to the foundation.
These two syllables have two foundations;
their secret name (*upaniṣad*) is "I" (*aham*). He who knows this destroys evil and is liberated from it. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.4)
In this same way, for this person who is in the right eye, everything beginning with "Bhūḥ is his head" is identical [to what was said of the other person].
His secret name (*upaniṣad*) is "Aham" (I),
because he is the innermost self (*pratyagātman*).
As before, this is because of the roots *hā* (to abandon) and *jahāti* (to leave). //4//
Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the commentary on the venerable Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
This person consists of mind and has light for its reality.
Within him, in the heart, he is like a grain of rice or a grain of barley.
He is the ruler of all, the lord of all; he governs all this, whatever exists.

Because limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are manifold and because that very Brahman under discussion possesses manifold attributes, the author, desiring to enjoin the meditation upon that same Brahman as qualified by the adjunct of the mind (*manas*), says: "Consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), meaning "mind-abounding," because it is perceived within the mind; and because one perceives with the mind, it is "consisting of mind. This Person is "light-true" (*bhāḥ satya*): light itself is the truth, the reality, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of which; thus he is "light-true," meaning luminous.
Because the mind has the nature of illuminating all objects and because it is composed of mind, it is luminous.
"In that inner heart" means within the heart;
the meaning is that it is seen by yogins in that inner heart as being of such a size as a grain of rice or a grain of barley, as if it were shrinking.

He is the Lord of all, the Lord and Master of everything that has arisen from his own differentiation. Even though he possesses lordship, he is not like others who are dependent on ministers and the like; rather, he is the Sovereign (adhipati), one who presides over and protects. He governs all this—whatever exists, whatever this entire world may be—he governs it all.
The fruit of the meditation on the mind-made [self] is indeed the attainment of that very form; for the Brāhmaṇa states: "In whatever way one meditates upon it, that very thing one becomes. (1)
Thus ends the sixth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the commentary on the venerable Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
"Lightning is Brahman," they say;
it is called lightning because of its flashing.
Lightning knows this one who knows thus: "Lightning is Brahman.
For lightning indeed is Brahman.

In the same way, another meditation on the True Brahman, which yields a distinguished fruit, is now begun: "They say, 'Lightning is Brahman. The etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of Brahman as lightning is stated: because it pierces (*vidānāt*), that is, because it cleaves through the darkness of the clouds by bursting asunder the gloom, it shines forth; therefore, it is called *vidyut*.

He who knows that Brahman is lightning endowed with such qualities—lightning pierces, cleaves, and destroys all those evils that have become adverse toward this Self; he [the knower] destroys all those evils.
For one who knows thus—that lightning is Brahman—the fruit is in accordance with that;
for indeed, lightning is Brahman. //1//
Thus ends the seventh Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the commentary on the venerable Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
One should meditate upon speech as a cow. It has four udders.
The utterance *svāhā*, the utterance *vaṣaṭ*, the utterance *hanta*, and the utterance *svadhā*— of her,
two breasts are those upon which the gods subsist:
the utterance *svāhā* and the utterance *vaṣaṭ*.
The *hantakāra* belongs to humans;
the *svadhākāra* belongs to the ancestors.
Of that [cow], the breath is the bull and the mind is the calf.

Furthermore, there is another meditation on that very same Brahman: "Speech is indeed Brahman. Speech is the word; it is a cow. Just as a cow is a "dhenu" because she flows with milk from her four teats for her calf, so too the cow of speech flows with food like milk from her teats—which are to be described hereafter—for the gods and others.
What, then, are those udders, or from which she flows?
Of this very cow of speech, two udders are lived upon by the gods who stand in the place of calves. Which two are they?
The utterance of *svāhā* and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*; for by these two the oblation is given to the gods. Humans [give] the utterance of *hanta*.
With the word "hanta," they offer food to human beings;
and with the utterances "svadhā" and "vaṣaṭ," for by these two the sacrificial oblation is given to the gods.
The *hantakāra* belongs to humans;
people offer food to humans with the words "Hanta! as well as with the *svadhākāra* and the *vaṣaṭkāra*, for by these two the oblation is given to the gods.
The *hantakāra* belongs to humans;
they offer food to humans with the word "Hanta.
The *svadhākāra* belongs to the ancestors.
For with the utterance of *svadhā*, they offer the *svadhā* oblation to the ancestors.
Of that speech-cow, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the bull;
for by means of the vital breath, speech is brought forth.
The mind is the calf;
for by the mind one is impelled,
and speech proceeds only toward an object that has been mentally perceived.
Therefore, the mind stands in the place of the calf;
thus, the one who meditates upon speech as the cow attains that very state which is to be realized. //1//
Thus ends the eighth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the commentary on the venerable Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
This Agni Vaiśvānara is that which is within the person,
by whom this food is digested.
Whatever is eaten here,
its sound becomes this which one hears when one covers the ears.
When he is about to depart, he no longer hears that sound.
This Vaiśvānara fire is another mode of meditation, as before.

As to what this Vaiśvānara fire is, he says: it is that which is within the person (puruṣa). Is it the fire that initiates the body? No; it is said to be that fire called Vaiśvānara by which this food is digested.
What is that food? That which is eaten and consumed by creatures is "food" (anna); the meaning is that it is the digestive fire (jaṭhara-agni).
To provide a direct illustration of this, he says: "Of that fire, as it digests food—that is, of the digestive fire—this sound arises."
Who is he?
He is that sound which one hears by covering the ears with the fingers—that is, by performing the act of closing them—and one should meditate upon that Prajāpati as the Vaiśvānara fire.
Here too, the fruit of meditation is becoming one with that very essence (*tādbhāvya*).
In this context, this incidental description of the signs of death (ariṣṭa) is stated: when he, the enjoyer within this body, is about to depart, he does not hear this sound. //1//
Thus ends the ninth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the commentary on the venerable Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
When a person indeed departs from this world, he goes to the wind; there the wind makes a way for him like the hole of a chariot wheel.
By that, he ascends upwards;
he reaches the sun;
for him, the sun makes way there.
Just as the sky is for a lambāra,
by that means he ascends upward;
he arrives at the moon.
Thereupon, he passes through it as easily as the sound of a drum through the air;
by that means, he ascends upwards.
He comes to that world which is free from sorrow and free from heat;
there he dwells for eternal years.
In this section, the destination and the fruit of all these meditations are stated: "When a wise person departs from this world, leaving the body, he then reaches the air;
in the intermediate space, the air remains motionless and impenetrable."
That wind, for its part, makes room for him who has arrived there within itself; it expands its own constituent parts and renders itself porous—this is the meaning.
As to what the dimension of that aperture is, it is said:
it is like the well-known dimension of the hole in the axle-hole of a chariot.
Through that opening, that wise one ascends; ascending, he goes upward and reaches the sun.
The sun stands having blocked the path for one desiring to go to the world of Brahman, yet it opens the door for the worshiper who knows thus.
For him, it yields there.
Just as the aperture of a particular musical instrument called a *lambara* has a certain dimension, by means of that he ascends upward and reaches the moon;
there too, it makes way for him.
Just as the aperture of a drum is well known, by means of that he ascends upward and reaches the world, the world of Prajāpati.
Of what nature is it?
It is "without sorrow," meaning it is devoid of mental suffering.
It is "without cold," meaning it is devoid of bodily suffering.
Having attained that, he dwells there for eternal, perpetual years—meaning for many kalpas of Brahmā. //1//
Thus ends the tenth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the commentary on the venerable Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
This indeed is the highest austerity: when one who is afflicted by illness undergoes the heat of fever. He who knows this wins the highest world.
This indeed is the supreme austerity: that they carry the deceased to the forest.
He who knows this wins the supreme world.
This indeed is the supreme austerity: that they place the deceased upon the fire.
He who knows this indeed conquers the supreme world. Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.11.1.
This indeed is the highest austerity.
What is that?
When one who is afflicted, diseased, or seized by fever and so forth undergoes suffering, one should reflect: "This is the highest austerity. Thus should he think.
Because of the commonality of suffering,

for that wise person who reflects in this way, that very austerity becomes the cause for the exhaustion of karma— provided he is blameless and does not despair. And he, having his impurities burnt away by that austerity of knowledge, indeed conquers the supreme world, provided he knows thus.
In the same way, this indeed is the supreme austerity: that they place the deceased upon the fire.
Because of the commonality of entering the fire, he who knows thus truly conquers the supreme world. //1//
Thus ends the eleventh Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the commentary on the venerable Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
"Food is Brahman," so some say;
that is not so.
"Food indeed putrefies without the vital breath (prāṇa).
'The vital breath is Brahman,' say some;
but that is not so."
"Indeed, the breath withers without food.
But these two deities, having become one, attain the supreme state.
Regarding this, Prātṛda once said to his father:
"What good could I possibly do for one who knows this? Or what evil could I possibly do to him?
He said, "Do not, O Prātṛda, touch me with your hand!
Who, having become a single unity of these two, attains the supreme state?"
Therefore, he said this to him:
"Vi. Food indeed is "vi," for all these beings are entered into (*viṣṭa*) in food.
"Ram. Breath indeed is "ram," for in breath all these beings find delight.
Indeed, all beings enter into him, and all beings delight in him, who knows thus. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.12.1)
"Food is Brahman.
Desiring to prescribe another such meditation, he says: "Some teachers say that food is Brahman because it is eaten; however, that should not be understood in that way—that food is Brahman.
Others say that breath is Brahman, but that also should not be understood in that way."
Why, then, should food not be grasped as Brahman?
Because, apart from the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it putrefies, decays, and reaches a state of corruption; how, then, can it be Brahman?
For that which is indeed called Brahman is that which is indestructible.
"Let it be, then, that the vital breath (prāṇa) is Brahman.
"Not at all," [he replied], "because the vital breath indeed withers away without food."
For the vital breath is the self; therefore, without food to eat, the self is unable to sustain itself.
Thus, it is said: "The vital breath indeed withers away without food."

Therefore, the state of being Brahman is not possible for either one individually; because of this, these two deities—food and breath—having become one, having attained oneness, reach the highest state, they attain the state of Brahman.
Having thus determined this, Prātṛda by name said to his father: "What indeed?"—the word *it-svit* expressing deliberation.
The intention is: "Since Brahman has been conceptualized by me in this way, what good could I possibly do for one who knows thus? What auspicious or beautiful act of worship could I perform for him?
And the intention is: "What indeed could I do that is not good for this knower? For he has already accomplished all that was to be done.
One who knows that food and vital breath are Brahman in union is not impaired by the performance of anything unwholesome.
Nor was he honored by the sound of applause.
To him who spoke thus, his father said, while warding him off with his hand: "Do not say so, Prātṛda; do not speak in this way.
Who indeed, having become a single unity of these two—food and breath—attains supremacy? No one at all; no wise man attains supremacy through this vision of Brahman."
Therefore, you should not say, "He has accomplished his purpose.
If you ask, "How then does he attain the supreme state?"—
to him he spoke these words that are about to be told.
What is that?
It is *vī*.
What is that *vī*?
It is said: "Food indeed is *vi*.
For because all these beings (*bhūta*) are entered into (*viṣṭa*), that is, supported by food, therefore food is called *vi*.
Furthermore, it is *ram*."
The father said, "Ram.
But what is that "ram"? "Prāṇa (vital breath) indeed is 'ram'."
Why is this so? He says:
For indeed, someone who lacks vital breath (*prāṇa*)—being without a dwelling place (*anāyatana*) and without support (*nirāśraya*)—does not find delight;
nor does one who lacks vital breath, even if a dwelling place exists, find delight when he is weak.

But when a living being possesses a [proper] abode and is strong, then the world rejoices, considering itself to have achieved its purpose, according to such scriptural passages as, "One should be young, a good youth, and a student of the Vedas. Now, he states the fruit for one who knows this: "Indeed, all beings enter into him because of his knowledge of the quality of food; all beings rejoice in him because of his knowledge of the quality of the vital breath—so it is for whoever knows thus. (1)
Thus ends the twelfth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the commentary on the venerable Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.13.1:
The Uktha.
The vital breath (prāṇa), indeed, is the Uktha.

For vital breath indeed raises up all this. A hero who knows the hymns (uktha) stands upright because of it; he who knows this wins union with the hymn and residence in the same world as it. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.13.1)
"Uktha":
likewise, another form of meditation is the *uktha*, which is a liturgical recitation;
for that is the principal element in the Mahāvrata sacrifice.
But what, then, is that Uktha? The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the Uktha.
Since the vital breath is the foremost among the sense organs and the Uktha among the liturgical recitations (śastra), one should meditate upon it as the Uktha.
How is it that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the *uktha*? He says: because the vital breath raises up all this;
since it causes [everything] to rise, the vital breath is the *uktha*. For no one who is without vital breath can rise up.
He states the fruit of that worship: "From one who knows thus, from one who knows the *uktha*, from one who knows the vital breath (*prāṇa*), a heroic son indeed arises; this is the seen fruit.
But as for the unseen fruit, he who knows thus conquers union with the *uktha* and residence in the same world as it. (1)
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.13.2:
The Yajus. Breath indeed is the Yajus.
For in breath all these beings are joined;
indeed, all beings are joined for his preeminence. He who knows this wins union with and residence in the same world as the Yajus. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.13.2.
One should meditate upon the vital breath (prāṇa) as the Yajus.
For the vital breath is indeed the Yajus. How is the vital breath the Yajus? [Because it joins together all things.]
For it is because all beings are joined together in the vital breath (prāṇa);
indeed, when the vital breath is absent, no one has the capacity for union with anything.
Therefore, because it joins [all things], the vital breath is the Yajus.
He states the fruit for one who knows thus: "They are joined" means they exert themselves.
For this knower, all beings strive for *śraiṣṭhya*—that is, for the state of being the best—for the sake of that state of being the best, thinking, "May he become the best among us.
The rest, beginning with "union with the Yajus, which is Prāṇa," is all the same as before. //2//
Sāman.
Breath indeed is Sāman.
For in breath all these beings are unified;
indeed, all beings become unified for the sake of his preeminence. He who knows this wins union with and residence in the same world as the Sāman. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.13.3)
One should meditate upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as *sāman*.
The vital breath is indeed *sāman*. How is the vital breath *sāman*?
For because all beings meet together (*samyañci*) in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and because it is the cause of their attaining equilibrium through that meeting, the vital breath is the *sāman*.
All beings meet together in him;
not only do they meet together, but they also become capable and are able to serve his state of excellence.
"Union with Sāman," and so forth, as before. //3//
The ruling power. The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the ruling power.
For the vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the ruling power (kṣatra); the vital breath protects him from being harmed. Thus, he attains the ruling power that wards off injury.
He who knows this wins union with and residence in the same world as Kṣatra. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.13.4.
One should meditate upon that vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the ruling power (*kṣattra*). Indeed, the vital breath is well known as the ruling power; for the vital breath is indeed the ruling power.
How is it well known? For the vital breath is indeed the ruling power.

How is it well-known? He says: because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) protects—that is, guards—this body (*piṇḍa*), when it is wounded by weapons or other means of injury, it replenishes it again with flesh; therefore, its status as *kṣattra* (the ruling power) is well-known from this protection of wounds (*kṣatatrāṇa*). He states the fruit for the knower: "The *kṣattra* does not protect itself by anything else"—that is, one attains the *kṣattra*, which is the vital breath, that is free from injury (*atra*).

Or, because it is read in another recension (śākhā), the meaning is that one becomes the vital breath (prāṇa) as mere ruling power (kṣattra). "He who knows thus wins union with and residence in the same world as the ruling power. //4//
Thus ends the thirteenth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the commentary on the venerable Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
"Earth, atmosphere, and heaven"— these are eight syllables.
Indeed, one foot of the *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables.
This, indeed, is her very foot.
Whoever knows this foot of hers in this way wins as much as there is in these three worlds. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.14.1)

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya 5.14.1: The meditation on Brahman as qualified by various limiting adjuncts (upādhi), such as the heart and so forth, has been described; now, the meditation on it as qualified by the Gāyatrī meter is to be stated, and thus this section begins.
For among all meters, the Gāyatrī meter is the most principal;
he will later state that it is called "Gāyatrī" because it protects (*gāyatrāt*) those who employ it.
Nor do other meters possess the capacity to protect the life-force of the user;
for she is the very self of the life-force, and the life-force is the self of all meters.
And it has been stated that the life-force is called *kṣattra* because it protects (*trāṇa*) from injury (*kṣata*).
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the *gāyatrī*;
therefore, the meditation upon it alone is intended to be taught,
both because it is the cause of birth as the best of the twice-born and because of its intrinsic nature.
He created the Brāhmaṇa from the Gāyatrī, the Rājanya from the Triṣṭubh, and the Vaiśya from the Jagatī; thus, for the best of the twice-born, the second birth is caused by the Gāyatrī.

Therefore, the Gāyatrī is preeminent. Having emerged as Brāhmaṇas [through it], they address one another: "That Brāhmaṇa becomes free from evil, free from passion, and free from doubt; he becomes a true Brāhmaṇa. Thus, the scripture demonstrates the connection of the Brāhmaṇa with the supreme human goal.
And since that status of being a Brāhmaṇa has its root in the birth from the Gāyatrī, the true nature of the Gāyatrī must be explained.

For the best of the twice-born, who is created by the Gāyatrī, is entitled without restriction to the means for achieving the supreme goal of man; therefore, the connection with that supreme goal has its root in her.
Consequently, for the purpose of prescribing her meditation, [the text] says: "Earth, intermediate space, heaven—these are the eight syllables."
That which has eight syllables—this is the "eight-syllabled" [Gāyatrī]. The particle *ha* indeed indicates well-known facts.
One is the first foot (*pada*) of the Gāyatrī.
The completion of the number eight is achieved by the syllable *ya* alone.
This indeed is that very first foot (*pada*) of this Gāyatrī, characterized by the earth and so forth, whose nature is the three worlds;
this is because of the commonality of having eight syllables.

Thus, for one who knows this first foot of the Gāyatrī, which consists of the three worlds, this is the fruit: whatever is to be conquered within these three worlds, all that indeed conquers the wise man who knows this foot of hers in this way. //1//
The *ṛc*s, the *yajus* formulas, and the *sāman* chants— these are eight syllables. Indeed, one foot of the *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables.
This, indeed, is its [the earth's] very essence.
As great as this threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā) is, so much does he conquer who knows this foot of it thus.
"The Ṛks, the Yajus, and the Sāmans"—these syllables of the threefold knowledge (*trayī-vidyā*) are likewise eight.

Thus, one foot of the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables; this [set of syllables] is indeed its second foot, precisely because it shares the commonality of having eight syllables, characterized as it is by the Ṛk, Yajus, and Sāman.

As great as this threefold knowledge is, and as great a collection of fruits as is obtained through that threefold knowledge—so much does he conquer who knows this foot of the Gāyatrī characterized by the threefold knowledge. //2//
"Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna"— these are eight syllables.
Indeed, one foot of the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables.
This, indeed, is her [the Earth's] very nature.
Whoever knows this foot of hers thus, he conquers as much as there is of living beings here.
Now, this is her fourth, visible foot, which shines beyond the dust—he who burns yonder [the sun].
That which is indeed the fourth is the *turīya*.
"The visible foot"—for it is, as it were, visible.
"Beyond the dust"—for this one indeed shines higher and higher above all the dust.
In this very way, he who knows this foot of hers thus shines with prosperity and fame. Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.14.3.
Likewise, *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *vyāna*—these syllables denoting the vital breaths and so forth are also eight.
And that is the third foot of the Gāyatrī; he who knows this third foot of the Gāyatrī in this manner conquers as much as this entire living world exists.

Next, the fourth foot of the three-footed Gāyatrī, which consists of sound, is being stated: it is the denotable object of this aforementioned Gāyatrī, namely, this very fourth foot which is about to be described as "the visible."

The Śruti itself explains the meaning of the words in the passage beginning with "the fourth" (turīyam) regarding that foot which shines beyond the dust (*parorajā*): "That which is well-known in the world as the fourth is what is denoted by the word *turīya*.

As for the meaning of the phrase "the visible foot" (*darśataṃ padam*), it is said: this Person who dwells within the solar orb appears as if he were visible; "beyond the dust" (*rajaḥ*) means beyond the entire world consisting of the realm of passion (*rajo-jātam*).
By virtue of its increasingly superior sovereignty, it scorches the entire world that has arisen as dust.
The repetition "uparyupari" (higher and higher) is for the purpose of making known its sovereignty over the whole world.
[Objection: Since this is already established by the word "all" (*sarva*), the repetition is redundant.
This is not a fault.
The repetition (*vīpsā*) is intended to dispel the doubt that the word "all" might refer only to those regions above which the sun is visible;
for the Śruti states: "And he rules over the worlds that are beyond that, and over the Devakas."
Therefore, the repetition is for the purpose of including everything.

Just as that sun shines with glory characterized by universal sovereignty, and with fame and renown, even so does he shine with glory and fame who knows this fourth, visible foot of it in this manner. //3//
This very Gāyatrī is established upon that fourth, visible foot, which is beyond the dust of the world;
and that, indeed, is established upon Truth.
The eye, indeed, is truth;
for the eye, truly, is truth.
Therefore, if two people should come disputing now, one saying "I saw" and the other "I heard," [the former would be the authority].
If someone were to say, "I have seen it," we would indeed place our trust in him alone;
for that truth is established upon strength.
Breath indeed is strength;
it is established in breath.
Therefore, they say that strength is more powerful than truth.
Thus, this Gāyatrī is established in the self (adhyātma). She protects the *gaya*s;
for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed the *gaya*s.
He established those vital breaths there; because he established the *gayas*, it is therefore called *gāyatrī*. That which he recites as the Sāvitrī is this very same one.
From whichever [verse] he recites, he thereby protects its vital breaths.

This very Gāyatrī, which was described as having three feet— characterized by the three worlds, the three Vedas, and the vital breath— is established in this fourth, supreme foot, beyond the dust of the mortal realm;
for the Sun is the essence of both the formed and the formless,
and when its essence is removed, an object becomes sapless and finds no firm foundation.
Just as wood and other materials are [useless] when their essence has been burnt,
so it is with the sun because its essence consists of both the formed and the formless;
for when the essence is gone, an object becomes sapless and unstable.
Just as wood and the like have their essence consumed by fire,

so too the world, consisting of both the formed and the formless, is established in the Sun— the Gāyatrī— along with its three feet, because it is the sap of that [Sun]. Indeed, that fourth foot is established in Truth.
What, then, is that truth? It is said: "The eye, indeed, is truth. How is the eye truth? He says: "This is well-known; for the eye, indeed, is truth.
How is it well-known? He says: "Therefore, if two people who are disputing and speaking in opposition were to come together and say, 'I saw this,' and..."

One person says, "I have seen it," while another says, "I heard that you saw it, but the object was not as [described]. Of these two, we should place our trust in the one who says, "I have seen it," and not in the one who says, "I heard it.
For a listener's hearing may be false, but the vision of the eye cannot be false.
Therefore, we would place our trust in one who says, "I did not hear it.
Thus, because truth is the cause for the attainment of reality, truth is the eye; the meaning is that the fourth quarter is established upon that truth-eye together with the other three quarters.
And it has been said: "In what is that sun established? "In the eye."

That truth, which indeed rests upon the fourth state (*turyapada*), is established in strength (*bala*). What, then, is that strength? He says: "Strength is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); in that strength, which is the vital breath, truth is established.
And so it is stated in the Sūtra: "In it [the Self], all this is woven like warp and woof."
Since truth is established upon strength, therefore they say that strength is more powerful than truth; "more powerful" (ogīya) means more vigorous (ojīya) or more intense (ojastara).
Even in the world, it is well known that whatever is dependent upon something else, the support is stronger than that which is supported.
Indeed, a weak thing is never seen to be the support for something strong.
By the logic thus stated, this Gāyatrī is established in the inner self—that is, in the vital breath (prāṇa).
This Gāyatrī is the vital breath;
therefore, the entire world is established in the Gāyatrī.

In that vital breath (*prāṇa*) wherein all the gods become one, and wherein all the Vedas, rituals, and their fruits are contained—that Gāyatrī, being the very form of the vital breath, is the Self of the world. She, indeed, protected (*tatré*) the *gaya*s; she has been a protector.
What, then, are the *gayas*? The vital breaths (*prāṇa*), beginning with speech, are indeed the *gayas*, because they produce sound (*śabda-karaṇāt*). That very Gāyatrī is [established] therein.
Because he sings (*gāyati*) there, therefore it is named *Gāyatrī*;
she is celebrated as *Gāyatrī* because she is sung.
That teacher, having initiated the eight-year-old boy, recites this very *Gāyatrī-Sāvitrī*—which has Savitṛ as its deity—in four-footed (*pāda*), half-verse (*ardharca*), and complete verse forms.

This very one is that Prāṇa, the manifest Self of the world, which has now been explained here as it was imparted to the young student (māṇavaka). It is none other than this. That teacher who recites and causes the student to recite protects (sāyate) the vital breaths (prāṇān) of that student from falling into hell and other such states. //4//
Regarding this, some recite this Sāvitrī as an Anuṣṭubh verse,
for speech is the Anuṣṭubh.
"We recite this speech," they say.
One should not do so;
one should rather recite the Gāyatrī Sāvitrī.
Even if one who knows this should indeed accept many gifts, it does not amount to even a single foot of the Gāyatrī.
Some followers of particular Vedic branches recite this Sāvitrī verse in the *anuṣṭubh* meter for the initiated student.
With reference to that, he says: "Speech is the *anuṣṭubh*.
And speech in the body is Sarasvatī; saying thus, they mean that they are reciting that very speech, Sarasvatī, for the boy.
One should not act in that way, nor should one know it thus; for what they say is indeed false.
What then? One should recite the Gāyatrī itself as the Sāvitrī.
Why?

Since it has been stated that "the vital breath (prāṇa) is the Gāyatrī," when the vital breath is mentioned, speech (vāk), Sarasvatī, and all those other vital breaths (prāṇas) are handed over to the student; everything becomes entrusted to him.
Furthermore, having said this as a digression, he praises the knower of the Gāyatrī: "Even if, indeed, one who knows thus [is] much... no, for not..."
That All-Self has many names; because it is the All-Self, whatever the learned man accepts does not suffice even for a single one of the four feet of the Gāyatrī. //5//

If one were to receive these three worlds filled with wealth, he would obtain only this first foot of hers. Furthermore, if one were to receive as much as there is of the threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā), he would obtain this second foot of hers.
Now, were anyone to take up as much as this living world, he would obtain only its third foot.
But its fourth foot— the visible one, which is beyond the dust and which shines yonder—
is by no means to be obtained by anyone at all.
How could he accept so much? Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.14.6.

If someone were to accept as a gift these three worlds— namely, those consisting of the earth and so forth, which are filled with wealth such as cows, horses, and the like— he who knows this Gāyatrī would thereby obtain this first foot of the Gāyatrī that has been explained; the fruit of knowing the first foot would have been enjoyed by him through that acceptance, but that acceptance would not produce any further fault.
Furthermore, if one were to receive as much of this threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā) as there is, he would obtain this third foot of it;
by that, the fruit of the realization of the third foot would have been enjoyed. This is stated as a conceptual construction.

Even if someone were to accept [the gift] equal to three-quarters [of the earth], that would be a cause for the exhaustion of the very fruit resulting from the knowledge of those three quarters, but it is not capable of being the agent of any other fault.
Neither the giver nor the recipient is like this;
rather, this is postulated as a praise for the knowledge of the Gāyatrī.
Even if the giver and the receiver are conceived in this manner, that acceptance is not susceptible to fault.
Why? Because there remains even more extensive knowledge of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), which belongs to the domain of the fourth quarter of the *Gāyatrī*; he shows that:
"Now, this is its very fourth, visible foot, beyond the dust—this which shines yonder."
And as for this [gift], it cannot be obtained by anyone through any means whatsoever, not even through acceptance; the meaning is that it is simply unattainable.

Just like the three steps mentioned previously, these too cannot be obtained by anyone. Having merely imagined them to be so, it was said [that he would accept]; but from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), how could one possibly accept such a thing, which is equal to the three worlds and so forth?
Therefore, the meaning is that the Gāyatrī itself is to be meditated upon in this manner. //6//
The prayer for her is:
"Gāyatrī, you are one-footed, two-footed, three-footed, four-footed."
You are trackless, for you do not leave a track.
Homage to your fourth, beautiful foot, which is beyond the realm of dust.
"May this one not attain that," or "May this desire not be fulfilled for him whom he hates"—
for him toward whom he thus pays homage, that desire indeed does not come to fulfillment.
or "I have reached that. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.14.7)
Regarding its worship: having approached the worship of that Gāyatrī—meaning the act of standing near and offering salutation—one should do so with this mantra.

He asks, "What is that mantra? and says: "O Gāyatrī, you are; you exist as one-footed by means of the foot consisting of the three worlds; as two-footed by means of the second form, which is the threefold knowledge (the Vedas);
and you are three-footed by means of the third, which consists of the vital breaths and so forth."

By the fourth, the supreme, you are four-footed; thus, through these four feet, you are stepped upon—that is, known—by the practitioners (*upāsakas*). Beyond that, by means of your own supreme, unconditioned self, you are "footless" (*apadasi*). You are footless because no foot exists for you by which you might be stepped upon, since you are the Self characterized as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*). Thus, you are indeed footless.
Therefore, [I bow] to the fourth, the visible state, which is the object of worldly discourse;
[I pray: "May that enemy, evil, which causes an obstacle to attaining you, not attain its own effect—namely, its status as an obstacle to attaining you.
The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the mantra.
Whomever one hates, against whom one should direct hatred, a wise person should perform this ritual attendance toward him, pronouncing his name: "This enemy is named so-and-so.
Or he performs the attendance with the thought: "May the desired wish for this Yajñadatta not come to fulfillment; may it not reach fulfillment.
For that wish does not indeed come to fulfillment for that Devadatta.
To whom?
To whichever [deity] one pays homage in this manner;
or one pays homage thinking, "I have obtained what was intended by Devadatta."
The three mantra-words beginning with "asāv ado mā prāpat" may be used optionally according to one's preference. //7//
Janaka of Videha said this to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi: "How is it that you, who claimed to be a knower of the Gāyatrī, are now carrying [me] as one who has become an elephant?"
"Indeed, O Emperor, I did not know her mouth," he said.
"Fire itself is her mouth.
For even if one throws much fuel into the fire, it consumes it all."
In this very way, even if one who knows thus should do much evil, it all becomes consumed; he becomes pure, cleansed, ageless, and immortal.
An explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) is now spoken for the purpose of prescribing the mouth of the *gāyatrī*: "This, indeed, is traditionally remembered.
In that regard, concerning the subject of the knowledge of the *gāyatrī*, Janaka Vaideha said to one named Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi—the son of Aśvatarāśva:

"Indeed, *yan nu* (if now)—this expresses a deliberation; *ho aho* (oh, alas!)—that which you, who claim to be a knower of the *gāyatrī*, said when you declared, 'I am a knower of the *gāyatrī*,' is this not inconsistent with that statement?"

Now, as to how it was that he said, "If you carry [the burden] because your hand has been paralyzed by the fault of accepting the gift of a *gāyatrī*," he replied, having been reminded by the king: "O King, it is because I did not know the mouth of this *gāyatrī*; indeed, I had not understood it.
He said, "Because of the deficiency of one limb, my knowledge of the *gāyatrī* has become fruitless."
Listen, then: fire itself is the mouth of that Gāyatrī.

Just as when people place even a great deal of fuel into the fire, the fire completely consumes all that fuel, even so, one who knows thus—knowing that "fire is the mouth of the Gāyatrī"—becomes himself the Gāyatrī-self with fire as its mouth.

Even if one commits many evils, such as the fault of accepting gifts and the like, having swallowed and consumed that entire collection of sins, he becomes pure and purified like fire; therefore, through the Gāyatrī, the self becomes ageless and immortal, free from the defect of accepting gifts. //8//
Thus ends the fourteenth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the commentary on the venerable Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
With a golden vessel, the face of Truth is covered.
