O Pūṣan, unveil it for me, who am devoted to the law of truth, so that I may see.
O Pūṣan, sole seer, Yama, Sūrya, son of Prajāpati! Spread out your rays and withdraw your splendor. I behold that form of yours which is most auspicious; that person who is yonder, that am I.
Vāyu is the breath, the immortal; and this body ends in ashes.
Oṃ! O Kratu, remember; remember what has been done; O Kratu, remember; remember what has been done. O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God, you who know all ways.
Keep away from us the crooked sin; we shall offer you the most abundant word of homage.
He who performs the combination of knowledge and ritual action prays to the Sun at the time of death.
And there is a relevant connection here, for that [Sun] is indeed the fourth foot of the Gāyatrī. Since its worship is the subject under discussion, it is that very one who is prayed to.

Just as a desired object is covered by a golden, luminous vessel, so too this Brahman called "Truth" is, as it were, covered by a luminous orb; because it is invisible to those whose minds are not concentrated, it is said that "the face of Truth is covered"—the "face" being its primary nature, and that "covering" being like a vessel-covering, the cause of obstruction to perception.
O Pūṣan, because you nourish the world, you are Pūṣan, the Sun; "uncover," that is, make open, remove the cause of obstruction to perception.
"To Satyadharma" means "to him whose nature is truth"; since that [truth] is my own nature, I am Satyadharma; "to him who has become your very self"—this is the meaning.
"For sight" means for the purpose of seeing.
"O Pūṣan," and so forth, are names of Savitṛ used for the purpose of address.
The "Single Seer" (ekarṣi) is one who is both single and a seer; he is a seer because of his vision.
For he, being the Self and the eye of the entire world, sees everything, or else he is the "Single Seer" because he moves alone, according to the Vedic verse: "The Sun moves alone.
O Yama, for the restraint of the entire world is accomplished by you.
O Sun, you manifest well the juices, the rays, the vital breaths, or the intellects of the world.
O Son of Prajāpati—whether the offspring of Prajāpati the Lord or of Hiraṇyagarbha—O Son of Prajāpati, spread out [your light], disperse your rays;
gather together and withdraw your splendor within yourself, so that I may be able to see your true nature directly.
Like a flash of lightning among forms, withdraw your radiance from this point.
I behold that form of yours which is the most excellent of all excellences, the most auspicious of all auspicious things;
we behold it by means of a grammatical substitution [of the singular for the plural].

That Puruṣa who consists of the constituent parts of the vyāhṛtis *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*—being Puruṣa by virtue of having a human form—is I; I am he. Because it is stated in the Upaniṣads that "I am He," this very same [Puruṣa] is referred to here with respect to both the solar and the ocular [forms]: "I am He, the Immortal. This is the connection. Upon the falling away of my body, let the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the wind residing within the body, go toward the external wind, that is, the atmosphere (*anila*).
Likewise, let the other deities return each to their own nature. Now, let this body also, having ended in ashes, go to the earth.
Now he prays to the deity Agni, who has become his own volition and resides in his mind: "Oṃ Krato!"
The words "Oṃ" and "Krato" are indeed for the purpose of address;
it is "Oṃ" because it is the symbol (pratīka) of Brahman,
and it is "Krato" because it consists of mind (manomaya).

"Oṃ! O Kratu, remember what is to be remembered; for at the time of death, by the power of remembering you, the desired goal is attained. Therefore, it is prayed: remember that which was performed by me—the repetition being for the sake of emphasis.
Furthermore, O Agni, lead us—bring us—by a beautiful path (*supathā*) to wealth (*rāye*), meaning for the attainment of the fruits of our actions.

Not by the southern, dark path which involves returning again, but rather by the bright, beautiful path alone, O God, you who know all the *vayunāni*, that is, the various forms of wisdom of all living beings."
Furthermore, drive away, remove, and separate from us all crooked sin—that is, the entire collection of evil deeds.
Freed from that sin, we shall proceed by the northern path through your grace.

However, as we are unable to perform service for you in the most abundant measure, let us offer you the greatest possible word of homage; that is to say, let us serve you with our utterance of salutation.
Being unable to do anything else. //1// //
Thus ends the fifteenth Brāhmaṇa of the fifth Adhyāya in the venerable Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. //5//
